references.text: The immediate context where Jesus asks the disciples to obtain swords, leading to their response in verse 38. Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 and explains that a new era has come in which they will face opposition.

When Jesus was arrested, one of the disciples used one of the two swords to cut off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus stopped the violence and healed the servant, showing that the swords were not meant for violent resistance. See Luke 22:49-51.

Matthew's parallel account of the sword strike at the arrest, where Jesus says, 'Put your sword back in its place! For all who draw the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:51-52). This emphasizes that Jesus did not want armed resistance.
John's account identifies Peter as the one who used the sword and Malchus as the one who was struck. Jesus orders Peter to put the sword back in its sheath (John 18:10-11).

The prophecy of the suffering servant who was 'numbered with transgressors,' which Jesus quotes in Luke 22:37 and which forms the background for the conversation about the swords. The disciples' possession of swords may have contributed to Jesus being regarded as a rebel leader.

Earlier, Jesus had sent the disciples out without any extra equipment—no staff, bag, bread, or money (Luke 9:3). The contrast with the instructions in Luke 22:36 shows that circumstances have now changed dramatically.

Paul emphasizes that 'the weapons we fight with are not of this world' (2 Corinthians 10:4). This sheds light on how the early church understood Jesus' words 'it is enough'—the Christian struggle is spiritual, not physical.

Paul refers to authorities as bearing the 'sword' (Romans 13:4) in their service. The sword motif in the New Testament has various shades of meaning, and Jesus' dismissive 'it is enough' in Luke 22:38 suggests that the disciples misunderstood his intention.
